lines.text: Conductor runs a team of coding agents on any codebase. On one of mine: 592 tasks, 197 agent hours, and 404 commits on main.
lines.say: Conductor runs a team of coding agents on any codebase. On one of mine: five hundred ninety two tasks, one hundred ninety seven agent hours, and four hundred four commits on main.

lines.text: Opus stays the manager. Over MCP it spawns up to eight opencode agents on free models like Space Bunny and GLM, so the grunt work never spends Opus usage.
lines.say: Opus stays the manager. Over M C P it spawns up to eight open code agents on free models like Space Bunny and G L M, so the grunt work never spends Opus usage.

lines.text: Each one gets a role, its own git worktree, and a locked list of files.
lines.say: Each one gets a role, its own git work tree, and a locked list of files.

lines.text: Then Opus waits on one shell command that returns the moment they finish, so its context stays clean.
Those agents went through about 20 billion tokens and over 45,000 tool calls, none of it spent on Opus.
lines.say: Those agents went through about twenty billion tokens and over forty five thousand tool calls, none of it spent on Opus.

lines.text: Every prompt puts its stable part first: the role, the skills and the repo map. So 95 to 99.97 percent of input came straight from cache.
lines.say: Every prompt puts its stable part first: the role, the skills, and the repo map. So ninety five to ninety nine point nine seven percent of input came straight from cache.

lines.text: It's a deliberate balance, tuned for security and speed: most work runs on its own, between Claude and Conductor.
I step in only for a gate, a paid model or a stuck task, and I can stop or steer any run at any time.
When a run finishes, Claude checks and verifies it, then merges it or flags it for me.
Rate limits skip to the next provider, and it's all one Python process.
